title: Negative numbers you will actually use
hook: A ship's meat room can be at −20 °C and its vegetable room at +4 °C. How many degrees apart are they, and why does 4 − (−20) give the same answer?
oneBreath: A negative number sits below a zero someone chose, and on an upright number line, drawn like a thermometer, higher up is bigger. A gap between two readings is never negative, but a change is last minus first, so a fall comes out negative. Adding a negative moves you down the line, and taking away a negative is the same as adding its opposite, so it moves you up. Multiplying by a negative turns the line half a turn about zero, so a negative times a negative is positive, and dividing follows the same signs because it undoes multiplying. Brackets come first, then powers, then times and divide, then add and take away, and a negative reading goes into a formula or a calculator inside brackets.

ideas.title: Below zero
ideas.oneLine: A negative number sits below a zero someone chose, and on an upright line higher up is bigger, so −5 °C is warmer than −18 °C.

ideas.title: Gaps across zero
ideas.oneLine: Count through zero to find the gap between two readings, and a gap is a distance, so it is never negative.

ideas.title: Adding
ideas.oneLine: Adding a positive number moves you up the line, and adding a negative number moves you down.

ideas.title: Taking away
ideas.oneLine: Taking away moves you down the line and on past zero when it must, so a change, last minus first, is negative when a reading falls.

ideas.title: Taking away a negative
ideas.oneLine: Taking away a negative is the same as adding its opposite, so 3 − (−2) = 5.

ideas.title: Multiplying
ideas.oneLine: Multiplying by a negative turns the line half a turn about zero, so one negative gives a negative answer and two give a positive.

ideas.title: Dividing
ideas.oneLine: Dividing undoes multiplying, so 12 ÷ −3 asks what times −3 makes 12, and the signs follow the rule for multiplying.

ideas.title: Order with negatives
ideas.oneLine: Work out brackets, then powers, then times and divide, then add and take away, so −3² is −9 while (−3)² is 9.

ideas.title: Formulas and your calculator
ideas.oneLine: Put a negative reading into a formula inside brackets, and key it in with the (−) key, not the take-away key.

calibration.q: At dawn a deck thermometer reads −12 °C, and by noon it reads +5 °C. How many degrees has it risen?
calibration.why: Count through zero: 12 degrees up to 0, then 5 more, so 17. Taking 5 from 12 gives 7, but that forgets the climb past zero, and a rise is never negative.
Start at −6 and go up 2: you reach −4, still below zero. 4 drops the minus sign, and −8 counts the 2 as a step down instead of up.
